headline: At the Frankfurt Book Fair, a row over a novelist accused of using AI has put proving who wrote a text at the centre of the debate, DW reports.
score_reason: Kept at 5: a useful snapshot of the publishing debate, but a feature built on one unproven allegation and varied opinion.
importance_line: Authors, publishers and readers are affected because it is hard to prove whether a text is AI-written, and one author's Goncourt nomination was withdrawn over allegations he denies.
summary: DW reports from the Frankfurt Book Fair that allegations that Haitian-Canadian author Thelyson Orelien's debut novel was written almost entirely with AI, which he denies, led to his Prix Goncourt nomination being withdrawn and have made proving who wrote a text a central question for publishing. DW adds that more than 140 German publishers have signed an appeal to Berlin and Brussels for stricter AI regulation, which so far remains only an appeal.
notes: Full DW text read. The AI allegation against the author is unproven; DW notes an AI tool made the claim and that 'we may never know for sure'.
